title: Vote to approve the Wilsonville Town Center Development District
ballot_label: Caption: Vote to approve the Wilsonville Town Center Development District. Question: Should the City adopt proposed Ordinance No. 905 establishing the Wilsonville Town Center Development District, an urban renewal district?
summary: Asks Wilsonville voters whether to adopt Ordinance No. 905 creating the Town Center Development District, an urban renewal district using tax increment financing to fund gathering spaces and parking, small-business incentives and infrastructure in Town Center. The plan sets maximum indebtedness of $152 million ($85.5 million in today's dollars) over a 28-year duration. The ballot summary states TIF is not a new tax or tax rate increase.
yes_means: A yes vote approves adoption of Ordinance No. 905, establishing the Wilsonville Town Center Development District as an urban renewal district.
no_means: A no vote rejects Ordinance No. 905, and the Town Center Development District urban renewal district would not be formed.
fiscal_impact: Per the county pamphlet explanatory statement: the Plan authorizes up to $152 million in principal indebtedness ($85.5 million in today's dollars), borrowed in portions over time, with tax increment collection anticipated for 28 years, through fiscal year 2056. The statement says the measure would not establish a new property tax or increase existing property tax rates, and that the accompanying report assumes taxable assessed value in the district could rise from about $206 million in 2027 to about $1.7 billion if forecast redevelopment occurs.

arguments.author: Shawn M. O’Neil, Wilsonville Mayor
arguments.statement: Mayor Shawn M. O'Neil argues that after years of planning the Town Center Plan should move to implementation, and that further delay carries costs.
arguments.excerpt: For nearly a decade, Wilsonville residents, businesses, volunteers, elected officials, and professional staff have invested extraordinary time and resources developing a vision for our Town Center. Now it is time to move from planning to implementation.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Sam Scull, Wilsonville City Councilor
arguments.statement: City Councilor Sam Scull argues Town Center redevelopment would improve streets, sidewalks, parks and public spaces and create opportunities for businesses, jobs and private investment.
arguments.excerpt: By making better use of land that’s already developed, we can improve streets, sidewalks, parks and public spaces while creating opportunities for new businesses, jobs and private investment.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Susan Reep (signed Susan Reep and Mark Smith)
arguments.statement: Susan Reep and Mark Smith argue a yes vote puts the Town Center Plan into action gradually over several decades, with parking and green spaces included in the plans.
arguments.excerpt: A YES vote puts the Town Center Plan into action by creating the Town Center Development District. This long-term plan guides improvements gradually, over several decades

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Kristin Akervall
arguments.statement: Kristin Akervall argues Wilsonville should have a Main Street with gathering places and more local restaurants and businesses, with options to drive, walk, bike or take the bus.
arguments.excerpt: We shouldn’t have to leave Wilsonville to find the restaurants, hangout spots, and experiences we want. We can create those opportunities here, while supporting the businesses and community we already call home.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Michele Gila, Portland Metro Association of REALTORS®
arguments.statement: The Portland Metro Association of REALTORS argues the measure funds public improvements that can support homeownership options and private investment in Town Center.
arguments.excerpt: Measure 3-641 provides an important tool to make those public improvements, unlocking the private investment that delivers the shops, restaurants, and gathering spaces the community deserves.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Bill Bagnall
arguments.statement: Bill Bagnall argues the Town Center Plan would let downsizing residents stay in Wilsonville near walkable amenities, and says it would not bring new taxes.
arguments.excerpt: The Town Center Plan allows residents who are downsizing to remain in Wilsonville and enjoy a safe, pleasant and relaxed quality of life with an intergenerational mix that creates dynamic and connected communities.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Adam Cunningham, Wilsonville City Councilor
arguments.statement: City Councilor Adam Cunningham argues the city's own projections point to a high-density apartment district, and that the measure authorizes up to $152 million in urban renewal debt.
arguments.excerpt: Measure 3-641 asks voters to authorize up to $152 million in urban renewal debt, repaid through 2056.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Katie Dunwell & Jennie Hill
arguments.statement: Katie Dunwell and Jennie Hill say they are voting no on the urban renewal financing plan, citing the debt and the housing density assumptions, and say the decision belongs to voters.
arguments.excerpt: We are voting no on the Town Center urban renewal financing plan. We are not convinced that taking on this debt to finance high density housing in Town Center is the right move for Wilsonville right now

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Rick and Elizabeth Peters
arguments.statement: Rick and Elizabeth Peters argue the measure would bring substantial new housing density and more traffic and commit the city to up to $152 million in indebtedness.
arguments.excerpt: This measure authorizes up to $152 million in indebtedness over 28 years, relying on future property tax growth to fund an ambitious slate of public projects.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Eric Winters, Keep Wilsonville Voting
arguments.statement: Eric Winters, for Keep Wilsonville Voting, argues the measure would use urban renewal to subsidize new apartments, adding traffic and committing future property taxes to city debt.
arguments.excerpt: It would use urban renewal to subsidize thousands of new apartments in Town Center, adding more traffic to already congested roads while committing millions in future property taxes to new City debt.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: Doris A. Wehler
arguments.statement: Doris Wehler argues the $152 million in debt would require about $174.5 million in urban renewal taxes over 28 years to subsidize private redevelopment.
arguments.excerpt: The City is asking us to approve $152 million in urban renewal debt, requiring approximately $174.5 million in urban renewal taxes over 28 years, to subsidize infrastructure, property acquisition and other costs of this massive private redevelopment.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

arguments.author: T.J. Reilly, Oregon Small Business Assocation [sic]
arguments.statement: T.J. Reilly of the Oregon Small Business Association argues tax increment financing diverts property-tax growth and could subsidize competitors of existing Town Center businesses, such as through food cart incentives.
arguments.excerpt: Tax increment financing diverts growth in property-tax revenues to finance development within the district. Existing businesses help generate those taxes whether the resulting projects help them or hurt them.

verification.note: Excerpt found verbatim in the cited source; side, sponsor and pamphlet order confirmed.

gaps: The county voters' pamphlet printed 19 arguments in favor (extract pages 69-78; printed C-68 to C-77). Six were recorded in pamphlet order (cap 6 per side); 13 further arguments in favor are not recorded, including those furnished by Chris Heydemann (Neighbors for Wilsonville), Andrew Engel, Mary Rooney, Christie Mayer, Rick Wallace, Erio E. Hoem, Caroline Berry, Jason Jones, Frank Garcia Jr. and Bill Bagnall (second argument).

The county voters' pamphlet printed 21 arguments in opposition (extract pages 78-88; printed C-77 to C-87). Six were recorded in pamphlet order (cap 6 per side); 15 further arguments in opposition are not recorded, including those furnished by Bryan Smith, Rod and Valorie Boucher, Kristin Roche, Kate Johnson, Robyn M. Rebers, Ned and Glenda Walls, Dwight Sims, John Ludlow, J. Michele Seal, Steve Gaschler, Steve Schopp, Jason Williams (Taxpayers Association of Oregon), Becky L. Fromhart, Kristi Corno (City of Wilsonville Parks & Rec Advisory Board) and Eric Winters (second argument).

Endorsements: sponsors of the first 12 filed arguments on each side (pamphlet order) are recorded, 24 of the 25 allowed. Not recorded: further yes sponsors Andrew Engel, Mary Rooney, Frank Garcia Jr. (repeat sponsors Bagnall, Heydemann, Mayer, Engel omitted as duplicates); further no sponsors Dwight Sims, John Ludlow, J. Michele Seal, Steve Gaschler, Steve Schopp, Jason Williams (Taxpayers Association of Oregon), Becky L. Fromhart, Kristi Corno (City of Wilsonville Parks & Rec Advisory Board).
